verdict.rationale: Official MoQ libraries cover web (TypeScript, e.g. @moq/watch and @moq/net) and iOS (Swift async sequences). FFI bindings include Kotlin, which implies Android support, and a production user reports browser, desktop and mobile clients all publishing to one relay. However, Android is never named, Kotlin support is an FFI binding rather than a dedicated SDK, and a shared session/track model across platforms is only implied by the common Rust core. Missing for 10: an explicitly documented Android SDK, documentation that the session/track model is identical across web, iOS and Android, and hands-on corroboration of Android clients.

support.subject: As a developer, official client SDKs cover web, iOS, and Android with the same session and track model, so one backend serves every platform

citations.quote: Libraries for Rust (native) and TypeScript (web), plus FFI bindings for C, Python, Kotlin, Swift, Go, and Dart.
Async sequences for iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.
Chat, game state, telemetry, and control channels over the same relays with [`moq-net`](/lib/rs/moq-net.html) or [`@moq/net`](/lib/js/net.html).
Browser, desktop, mobile and device clients publish Opus to one relay, which fans out to independent subscribers
